sources.entry: An introduction to distributed systems - Kyle Kingsbury *(aphyr, author of Jepsen)*

summary.one_liner: An outline of Kyle Kingsbury's (aphyr) 16-32 hour introductory distributed systems class, covering theory, algorithms, and practical design concerns, with optional labs.
summary.what_it_does: The README is the written outline for a practitioner-oriented distributed systems class. It covers theory first: nodes, synchronous versus asynchronous networks, failure modes such as drops, delays, duplicates and Byzantine behavior, and TCP versus UDP. It then covers clocks (wall, Lamport, vector), consensus protocols (Paxos, ZAB, Viewstamped Replication, Raft), and transaction architectures (single-writer, Percolator, Spanner, Calvin). Later sections survey characteristic latencies from multicore to geographic replication, common system types (KV stores, SQL, search, queues, streaming), and design patterns such as avoiding distribution, redundancy, sharding, immutability, backpressure, and service boundaries. The document is an outline with terse bullet points and references to papers, not a tutorial or code project.
use_cases: preparing a team training session on consensus and clocks
deciding whether to use a distributed queue or plain TCP
reviewing trade-offs between Paxos, Raft, and ZAB
reading a checklist of design patterns for sharding and redundancy
understanding why wall clocks are unreliable across nodes
notable: Written by Kyle Kingsbury (aphyr), author of Jepsen, and framed for practitioners rather than researchers
Organized as a map of concepts with paper references (Lamport, Ongaro and Ousterhout, Junqueira et al., Van Renesse) for further reading
Compares real systems to each concept, e.g. Chubby, Cassandra, etcd, Consul, Kafka, Spanner, Calvin/Fauna, and TiDB
Includes anecdotal caveats such as NTP clock jumps and the 2017 Cloudflare leap-second incident
Opinionated design rules such as 'don't distribute where you don't have to' and 'use TCP first'
caveats: The README is a truncated outline; it is not a complete course, and the text itself says it accompanies a live class
Labs are referenced but not included in this repository's README
Many statements are opinions and anecdotes (e.g. 'hearsay', 'YMMV'), and some sections are unfinished or have blank bullets
